content_html:
Hey! @cart here (Bevy's creator and Project Lead). It is crazy to say it, but Bevy is six years old now!

As is tradition, I will take this as a chance to reflect on the past year and outline our hopes and dreams for the future. If you're curious, check out Bevy's First, Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth birthday posts.

I highly encourage Bevy developers and community members to write their own Bevy's Sixth Birthday reflection posts. Just publish your post somewhere (and to social media if you want) and link to it here. One month from now, we will do a "Reflecting on Bevy's Sixth Year" rollup post that aggregates these in one place. This is our chance as a community to celebrate our wins, identify improvement areas, and calibrate our path for the next year.

For those who don't know, Bevy is a refreshingly simple data-driven game engine and app framework built in Rust. Bevy is also free and open source forever! You can grab the full source code on GitHub. We have a Quick Start Guide. You can check out Bevy Assets for a library of community-developed plugins, crates, games, and learning resources.

This is all made possible by the Bevy Foundation's generous donors. If you enjoy Bevy, please consider supporting our work! Every donation goes directly toward improving Bevy for everyone, and we are drastically underfunded for our ambitions.

A Year of Milestones #

  • August 25: Bevy Merch
    • We launched our new Bevy Merch store so Bevy developers can show their support. Note that we only make $3 on each sale ... the primary purpose of the store is to allow people to rep Bevy out in the wild, not to be a funding source.
  • September 30: Bevy 0.17
    • We landed Solari / Raytraced Lighting, Improved Observers / Events, core Bevy UI Widgets, Bevy Feathers, Rust Hotpatching, Light Textures, DLSS, Tilemap Chunk Rendering, Web-hosted Asset Loading, Reflect Auto-Registration, Frame Time Graphs, UI Gradients, Raymarched Atmosphere, Virtual Geometry, BVH Culling, and more!
  • December 10: Bevy Metrics
    • Thanks to our generous donors and François' efforts, we landed an automated metrics system that runs on every Bevy commit, tracking Bevy's runtime performance, compile times, and binary sizes over time. This has helped us catch a ton of regressions and will be a key piece of infrastructure for us going forward.
  • January 13: Bevy 0.18
    • We landed Atmosphere Occlusion and PBR Shading, Generalized Atmospheric Scattering Media, Solari Improvements, PBR Shading Fixes, Font Variations, Automatic Directional Navigation, Fullscreen Materials, Cargo Feature Collections, First Party Camera Controllers, and more!
  • February 7: Bevy Jam #7
    • The seventh official Bevy game jam! 310 people joined, 64 people submitted games, and people left 1,331 ratings. The theme was Extremely Incohesive Fever Dream, and the participants really took that to heart. The delightfully chaotic (and surprisingly complete) PvF won. You should check it out!
  • April 1: Bavy Jam #1
    • To celebrate April Fools we had our first ever Bavy Jam, with no warning and a 24 hour duration to test BSN before it released. Developers had to use Bevy's main branch to build something rat themed :)
  • June: Bevy hit 6,000,000 downloads on crates.io!
  • June 19: Bevy 0.19
    • We landed Next Generation Scenes/ BSN, Render Bigger Scenes Faster, Contact Shadows, More Feathers Widgets, Text Input, Richer Text, App Settings, Post Processing Effects, Improved Skinned Mesh Culling, and more!
  • August 10: Bevy is now six years old!

A Year By The Numbers #

  • 1,527 unique Bevy contributors on GitHub (up from 1,291)
  • 47,529 GitHub stars (up from 40,900)
  • 5,189 forks on GitHub (up from 4,429)
  • 16,415 pull requests (12,501 merged) on GitHub (up from 12,928 prs and 9,795 merged)
  • 9,348 issues (6,373 closed) on GitHub (up from 7,829 and 5,316 closed)
  • 13,543 commits on GitHub (up from 10,831)
  • 1,830 GitHub Discussions (up from 1,684)
  • 501 Bevy Assets (plugins, crates, games, apps, and learning materials) (up from 442)
  • 6,656,483 downloads on crates.io (up from 2,753,203)
  • 23,359 Bevy Discord members (up from 21,985)
  • 6,906 community #showcase entries in the Bevy Discord (up from 5,697)
  • 3,751,524 messages in the Bevy Discord (up from 2,836,825)

Note that for consistency and clarity all of these numbers are given in "absolute totals", as that is how they are generally reported. For example, we now have 47,529 total GitHub stars ... the number you will see in our repo. I've included the totals as reported last year as well, which can be used to calculate the change in the numbers since last year.

Things I'm Proud Of #

I always try not to repeat myself here, but note that I am still extremely proud of the things I outlined in Bevy's First, Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth) birthday posts.

BSN #

This year we finally landed BSN: Bevy's next generation scene system:

This was a massive step forward for Bevy's usability. It enables developers to quickly and easily spawn composable, inheritable, interrelated hierarchies of ECS entities and components in a templated, dependency and asset-aware way (some engines call these "prefabs" instead of "scenes"). Developers can compose BSN within their Rust code using the bsn! macro, or they can define it in asset files (the .bsn asset format should land on Bevy main soon).

BSN is also a key piece of Bevy's UI story going forward. UI developers (especially outside of the engine space) expect a certain level of ergonomics that raw Rust cannot provide. With BSN, composing UI in Bevy has never been easier!

fn button() -> impl Scene {
    bsn! {
        Node { width: px(200), height: px(100) }
        on(|press: On<PointerPress>| info!("pressed!"))
        Children [
            Text("Button")
        ]
    }
}

Unlike other popular UI frameworks, BSN is a general purpose ECS-powered data layer, equally useful for game logic, general purpose app logic, and UI logic.

BSN is pivotal for the upcoming Bevy Editor, which will be a normal Bevy app built on top of Bevy UI + BSN. The Bevy Editor will also compose BSN assets via a visual scene editor.

I'm really happy to see people enjoying BSN in the wild. Exofactory's developer saved 7,364 lines of code after porting their spawning code to BSN. BSN was a multi-year project for me and finally getting "real world" value out of it feels so good.

I'll let the blog post explain the BSN details, but this is an exciting time to be a Bevy dev!

Bevy UI #

Bevy's UI story came a long way this year. In addition to landing BSN, we landed our "core Bevy UI widgets", which are behavior-only "style-less" widgets, intended to be used as the shared baseline for styled / higher level widgets. Add the Button widget to your entity, and it starts behaving like a button, with button events, press and hover states, keyboard shortcuts, and accessibility features!

fn button() -> impl Scene {
    bsn! { 
        Button
        Node { width: px(200), height: px(100) }
        on(|activate: On<Activate>| {
            info!("Button activated!")
        })
    }
}

We landed buttons, checkboxes, radio buttons, lists, scroll areas / scroll bars, sliders, modal dialogs, menus, and popovers. We also finally landed an upstream text input widget:

Bevy UI now also supports gradients, per-side UI border colors, text background colors, automatic directional navigation, font variations like strikethroughs, underlines, weights, and ligatures, variable font properties, and better font selection.

Things are starting to get quite functional in Bevy UI land!

Bevy Feathers #

We also landed Bevy Feathers early this year (led by Talin), and then significantly evolved and expanded it throughout the year. Bevy Feathers is our opinionated "dev tools" widget set, which builds on the "core Bevy UI widgets" mentioned above.

We're using these widgets to build the Bevy Editor, in addition to things like an ECS inspector, debug menus, etc.

Bevy Rendering Devs Go Hard #

This year was packed with renderer work. We landed and evolved Solari, our experimental real-time raytraced renderer (led by Jasmine):

This was a MASSIVE year for GPU-driven rendering (led by @pcwalton). On modern hardware, Bevy can now handle huge scenes; drawing millions of entities at playable framerates. Our new bevy_city example is a great real world test. It procedurally generates a city with (by default) 55,000 entities (including moving cars) and it can render at 60fps! This requires no special "performance" APIs, just the standard easy-to-use data-driven Bevy APIs.

We've also started landing "renderer unification" work. Bevy's 3D rendering is quite advanced at this point, and we'd like our 2D renderer to share the same infrastructure and benefit from all of the work we've done.

A few days ago we fully adopted WESL shaders (migrating away from our custom-built WGSL dialect). WESL extends WGSL to support modules / imports and first class conditional compilation. It has a native Rust toolchain which builds "by default" with no specialized configuration, and we can deploy it "anywhere". We've been collaborating closely with the WESL team to shape the specification and ensure it is a great fit for Bevy.

import package::{color::palette, shape::star};
import lygia::{draw::fill::fill, generative::snoise::snoise2};
import env::u;

@fragment
fn main(@builtin(position) pos: vec4f) -> @location(0) vec4f {
  let uv = pos.xy / u.resolution;
  var sdf = star(pos.xy, u.resolution);

  @if(noise)  // conditions at runtime or build time
  sdf += snoise2(uv * 8.0 + u.time) * 0.15;

  let shape = fill(sdf, 0.6);
  return vec4f(palette(uv, u.time) * shape, shape);
}

The current baseline implementation is a marked improvement over the old Bevy shader experience, but this is just the beginning. They're in the process of building out features like generics, which will allow us to make high level Bevy material shaders much more accessible than they currently are. We're aiming to have a unique "best of all worlds" cohesive implementation that makes the easy stuff easy, without hiding the details away from the tinkerers (in classic Bevy fashion).

We also landed a ton of renderer features: our virtual geometry ("nanite") implementation got BVH culling, we landed DLSS support, contact shadows, physically based screen space reflections, rectangular area lights, light textures, real-time filtered environment maps, vastly improved our atmosphere rendering, and fixed some of the "PBR rendering quirkiness" that has plagued us for awhile.

Jackdaw: The Community-Driven Bevy Editor Experiment #

This year we continued to lay the foundations for the Bevy Editor upstream. While we did this, members of the Bevy community (led by @jbuehler23) started using these foundations (BSN, Bevy Remote Protocol, Bevy UI, Bevy Feathers) to build out a functional Bevy Editor prototype called Jackdaw. Jackdaw is becoming dangerously functional:

It already has a visual BSN scene editor, ECS inspection, undo/redo, a dynamic plugin / extension loading system, a material system, terrain editing, a project manager / creator, and geometry editing tooling.

They've done a great job of mapping the space and exercising Bevy's foundations in practice. Once we land a couple more foundational pieces upstream (such as Assets as Entities and .bsn asset support), we'll spin up the Bevy Editor Working Group, where I plan on focusing my attention on guiding upstream Bevy Editor development, collaborating with the Jackdaw devs to take the best ideas from Jackdaw and finally for real this time build Bevy's official editor.

Bevy Metrics #

Tracking performance, compile time, and binary size regressions in a game engine is critical. Historically, we have done this manually "as needed". Thanks to our generous donors and François' efforts, we landed Bevy Metrics: an automated metrics system that runs on every Bevy commit, tracking Bevy's runtime performance, compile times, and binary sizes over time. This has already helped us catch a ton of regressions and will be a key piece of infrastructure for us going forward.

Bevy Project Goals #

Bevy development is very "ad hoc". Each individual works on what they want to, when they want to. It has historically been hard to track what is currently going on in the project, what our priorities are, what our priorities aren't, and where project leadership is currently focusing their attention. This created a lot of unnecessary tension, as contributors would often spend months building something, only to hit a wall because they built the "wrong" thing, or because project leadership didn't have the time to give the contributor's effort the attention it needed to be shepherded upstream. Additionally, Bevy community members (and people interested in Bevy) often asked for a "roadmap", and we'd say "we don't have one" and "that is not how we do things here".

This year I formulated and enacted the light-weight Bevy Project Goals system, which aims to give us the tools we need to prioritize work and collaborate on that work together (check out our Contributor Guide for details). The community can propose new Goals, and we discuss those proposals on a weekly basis to decide if we want to approve, deny, or postpone them. It also allows members of project leadership (the Project Lead ... me, SMEs (Subject Matter experts), and Maintainers) the ability to "staff" Goals, which provides a signal to the community that this Goal is "fast tracked" and will receive immediate attention and stewardship.

This allows leadership to be honest about its capacity (we can't "staff" everything at once) and its priorities (there are some things we must focus on, and some things we should not focus on).

This is notably not a "roadmap". We aren't meaningfully planning the order of future steps ahead of time. We are just communicating the current state of things. This is also not authoritative. The Bevy community is still free to build whatever it pleases, whenever it pleases. We just now have a way to collectively decide our direction and create the necessary contribution on ramps and infrastructure to collaborate (ex: Working Groups).

I am personally very happy with Goals (especially their current iteration), and believe they were an important missing piece of our workflow. The rollout wasn't quite as smooth as it should have been (which I'll touch on in the next section).

Real Projects™ Using Bevy #

This year we had a ton of new Bevy usage, with some exciting Steam releases, demos, and non-game apps.

  • Toroban: an infinitely wrapping puzzle game, was released on Steam.
  • Exofactory: a factory building game in a chill open world, made significant progress and had a ton of interesting devlogs.
  • Jarl: a fantasy colony simulation game is running playtests at the moment.
  • Polders, a historical Dutch city builder, continued to make significant progress this year.
  • Wee Boats The chill multiplayer boaty honk game, now has a demo on steam!
  • Sven is building a spaceflight simulation game
  • Foresight (one of Bevy's biggest sponsors) is using Bevy to build Foresight Spatial Engine (already used in production) and SpatialDrive a database built for interacting with and visualizing 3D time series data.
  • Nominal: is building hardware test apps for real-time automation, analysis, and data capture at the edge.
  • Gob Johnson's Downhill Marmalade: a fast-paced slalom 'em up fantasy roguelite, released on Steam.
  • Simulo, a multiplayer 2D physics sandbox, released on Steam.
  • Insanio: an autobattler where you send misfits into vehicular combat, released on Steam.
  • Court Wizard: A roguelite where you cast spells to defend the kingdom, was released on Steam.
  • Willcaster: a game where you guide an ordinary frog on your magical game board, helping him with your spells, was announced on Steam.
  • Unhaunter: the paranormal investigation simulator, made a lot of progress this year.
  • One Planet: a political strategy game where you take on climate change, was announced on Steam.
  • Manufact: a "design for manufacture" and simulation platform, was released. It uses Bevy as the renderer!

bevy_awesome_prod has even more cool projects!

There Is Always Room For Improvement #

The Goal System Rollout #

The initial rollout and framing of Bevy Project Goals caused some (well-founded) concern and anxiety in the community, as it was phrased in a way that made it feel "dictatorial". One of my Goals for the system was to establish "boundaries". Historically, our process (and lack thereof) organically created a culture of "build first, then yell for attention until you get it". Leadership was constantly derailing itself from its priorities to shepherd whatever happened to land on our doorstep, and this created situations such as continually promising that the Bevy Editor was a priority, yet it never manifesting over the course of many ... many years. That particular case is a complicated, multi-dimensional problem, but prioritizing the upstreaming of arbitrary unrelated work was a big piece of the problem.

This culture bred toxicity in a number of ways. It created resentment in me whenever a new (very cool) thing landed on our doorstep that pulled me away from the work that I strongly believed Bevy needed. It created burnout and feelings of betrayal in contributors when their work was left unreviewed indefinitely. It created disillusionment in the wider community when critical foundational pieces (such as BSN) dragged on for years (that particular case is also multi-dimensional ... I could have pushed my work publicly years earlier and embraced public community development rather than polishing it slowly on my own).

These were fundamentally problems of communication. Project leadership only has so many hours in the day. We have the right (and responsibility) to choose how we want to spend them. What the project desperately needed was a way to communicate them.

Project Goals were initially framed in a way that focused on that. Preventing working from being done that wasn't "aligned" or "prioritized". Working Groups could only be created for efforts that were currently "staffed" by leadership. Goals were only "active" if they were "staffed", and "unstaffed" Goals were "inactive". While I do think this type of prioritization is necessary to a degree, it was ham-fisted and didn't properly respect Bevy's "organic development culture".

We've (very recently) adopted a looser approach. "Staffed" and "unstaffed" are the states (rather than "active" and "inactive"). Working Groups can be formed for any "approved" Goal, even if it is not currently staffed. I believe this strikes the right balance. The community can propose work and collaborate on anything that is approved. We can provide these people with the centralized collaboration infrastructure they need (Working Groups), and they can make progress with or without us. However "staffing" still serves as a signal to the community as to where we are directing our focus, so it can set its expectations accordingly.

AI Policy #

AI has been a constant stressor on the Bevy community this year. We adopted a strict "no-AI" policy this year, which solved many problems but created many others (including fostering toxic witch hunts, incentivizing lying to maintainers, enforcement was a hard / impossible task). We are all very tired and emotionally raw.

@alice-i-cecile has been working with the community (including me) to draft a new policy. I'm pretty anti-AI myself, I don't use it in my development workflows (I love my craft and don't have much interest in outsourcing it), and I am deeply concerned about the risks of AI adoption when it comes to fostering a community of competent engine developers. I think the new policy strikes the correct balance for our community. We haven't released a new policy yet (we are still working on it) and we aren't interested in starting a wider public conversation at the moment (aka: a conversation outside of the Bevy community). But I am optimistic that we are soon to be on the right track.

The Bevy Foundation is (Still) Under-Funded #

I outlined three paths to improve this last year: proactive fundraising, revenue generating services, and continuing to build the engine to make it more attractive and extend our reach. I didn't meaningfully do either of the first two this year. I did focus heavily on building out Bevy's foundations this year and avoiding sidetracking, and I think we are verging on a level of capability and elegance that will attract developers and funding in greater volumes. I don't think I should be focused on proactive fundraising or revenue generating services until the Bevy technology platform has reached a certain level of completeness, as that is where my competency lies, and I don't feel particularly comfortable evangelizing while there are still key pieces of the puzzle in flight.

We need more full time developers so we can move faster. We need to pay our existing developers baseline salaries that encourage them to stay (rather than the ~54% paycut relative to the baseline that we are paying them today). Please help us!

Did We Learn From Last Year? #

It is important for organizations (and leaders) to learn from their mistakes. Here is my list of "improvement areas" from last year's birthday post, followed by how I think we handled them this year:

BSN Should Have Landed Faster

I believe the core issue here (@cart developing in isolation for extended periods until things are "good enough" in my eyes) has largely been addressed. BSN development over the past year has been iterative and public. My work on Assets as Entities has evolved in the open and iteratively. I've been making lots of targeted, small, but high value changes to various parts of the engine that I've been wanting to for awhile, with instant feedback loops with the community. I do daily status updates so people can track what I'm currently working on. I'll try my hardest not to slip back in to old patterns, but I'm pretty happy with how things have played out recently. I'm curious to hear what everyone else thinks about this!

The Bevy Foundation is Under-Funded

I discussed this above. This is still a problem! Please support our work by donating to the Bevy Foundation!

Can @cart Predict The Future? #

In last year's birthday post I made some predictions for the next year. Let's see how I did!

BSN

We landed BSN. Score!

Reactivity Ecosystem

Bevy does have a reactivity ecosystem! There are BSN reactive impls like bevy_reactor and Jasmine's (rough / quick) reactive BSN experiment. There is also haalka, which uses "functional reactive programming" to produce its own (non-BSN, but Bevy-native) data API.

We haven't yet converged on the correct upstream implementation, but I suspect this will happen within the year now that Bevy UI, Feathers, and BSN are all in a pretty solid place.

Core / Standard UI Widgets

We landed these! Another win!

Baseline Editor Platform

We did not land a baseline editor platform upstream. As mentioned above, we have made solid progress on the foundations. The ECS Inspector working group has a functional inspector implementation. Jackdaw has successfully prototyped what an editor platform could look like. We made significant, tangible, usable progress toward the goal this year. I have been saying "Bevy Editor next year" for many years now. You probably shouldn't trust me when I say it is close now. But we now have the scene system, the UI system, the editor widget library, the asset system, the remote protocol, the design language and mockups, a proven dynamic plugin loading model, and an extremely functional prototype. Additionally, we finally have a Project Lead who has run out of prerequisites to block editor progress on (well ... after Assets as Entities, but that is wrapping up now). We are well positioned to break ground. That is our (and my) next and overriding priority. We can do this!

The Next Year of Bevy #

The Bevy Community and I take a relatively organic and reactive approach to developing Bevy. It doesn't make sense to outline a long list of "plans" when that isn't really how development works in practice.

That being said, here are some of my personal hopes, dreams, and personal priorities for the next year of Bevy:

  • Assets as Entities: This is what I'm currently working on (with @andriyDev). It is a key piece of the editor story, as we need to be able to express complex, nested, templated assets in BSN + the Bevy Editor, and Assets as Entities is what will allow that to happen, as BSN expresses complex, nested, templated entities. It will also vastly simplify our asset system internals, make asset events "observable / react-able", and generally make assets feel more cohesive with the rest of Bevy.
  • .bsn Asset Format: BSN landed with bsn! macro support. It also landed with "runtime" support for scene assets. It didn't land with the actual .bsn asset loader. The Bevy Editor will produce .bsn files, so this is a necessary piece to land. There is a draft PR for this out, although it needs some work. We should be able to land this shortly!
  • Upstream Bevy Editor MVP: We need this. You want this. We have proven implementations. We have prioritized progress at the cost of pretty much everything else. We are very, very close now.
  • Reactivity Ecosystem: As mentioned above, we have explored the space, we have built the other prerequisites. I'm relatively confident we can land something this year, but I'm personally prioritizing showing upstream progress on the Bevy Editor. Reactivity is likely a part of the final UI / Editor story, but I don't think we should block on it.
  • Excellent Shader and Material Workflows: We've been focused on modernizing the renderer and landing foundational pieces like WESL. However this has come at the cost of more user-facing shader / custom material complexity. Once the initial "2D / 3D renderer unification" work lands, I think we need to pivot our focus toward the user facing experience / lowering the accessibility bar of custom material shaders. @tychedelia has big plans for this space and I can't wait to see where this lands. WESL is a solid start, and should serve as a foundation for this work (especially as it evolves).

We have plenty of other work in the pipeline, but I'm once again choosing to keep this very focused this year to convey my personal priorities.

One last reminder that Bevy community members should write their own Bevy Birthday blog posts. Submit them here!

If any of this excites you, we would love your help! Check out our code on GitHub and start participating in the Bevy Community.

Also please consider donating to The Bevy Foundation to ensure we can continue building and leading this wildly ambitious project. The more funds we have, the more we can scale Bevy development!

To many more years of Bevy!

- @cart

I've included the totals as reported last year as well, which can be used to calculate the change in the numbers since last year.Things I'm Proud Of #I always try not to repeat myself here, but note that I am still extremely proud of the things I outlined in Bevy's First, Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth) birthday posts.BSN #This year we finally landed BSN: Bevy's next generation scene system:This was a massive step forward for Bevy's usability. It enables developers to quickly and easily spawn composable, inheritable, interrelated hierarchies of ECS entities and components in a templated, dependency and asset-aware way (some engines call these "prefabs" instead of "scenes"). Developers can compose BSN within their Rust code using the bsn! macro, or they can define it in asset files (the .bsn asset format should land on Bevy main soon).BSN is also a key piece of Bevy's UI story going forward. UI developers (especially outside of the engine space) expect a certain level of ergonomics that raw Rust cannot provide. With BSN, composing UI in Bevy has never been easier!fn button() -> impl Scene { bsn! { Node { width: px(200), height: px(100) } on(|press: On<PointerPress>| info!("pressed!")) Children [ Text("Button") ] } }Unlike other popular UI frameworks, BSN is a general purpose ECS-powered data layer, equally useful for game logic, general purpose app logic, and UI logic.BSN is pivotal for the upcoming Bevy Editor, which will be a normal Bevy app built on top of Bevy UI + BSN. The Bevy Editor will also compose BSN assets via a visual scene editor.I'm really happy to see people enjoying BSN in the wild. Exofactory's developer saved 7,364 lines of code after porting their spawning code to BSN. BSN was a multi-year project for me and finally getting "real world" value out of it feels so good.I'll let the blog post explain the BSN details, but this is an exciting time to be a Bevy dev!Bevy UI #Bevy's UI story came a long way this year. In addition to landing BSN, we landed our "core Bevy UI widgets", which are behavior-only "style-less" widgets, intended to be used as the shared baseline for styled / higher level widgets. Add the Button widget to your entity, and it starts behaving like a button, with button events, press and hover states, keyboard shortcuts, and accessibility features!fn button() -> impl Scene { bsn! { Button Node { width: px(200), height: px(100) } on(|activate: On<Activate>| { info!("Button activated!") }) } }We landed buttons, checkboxes, radio buttons, lists, scroll areas / scroll bars, sliders, modal dialogs, menus, and popovers. We also finally landed an upstream text input widget:Bevy UI now also supports gradients, per-side UI border colors, text background colors, automatic directional navigation, font variations like strikethroughs, underlines, weights, and ligatures, variable font properties, and better font selection.Things are starting to get quite functional in Bevy UI land!Bevy Feathers #We also landed Bevy Feathers early this year (led by Talin), and then significantly evolved and expanded it throughout the year. Bevy Feathers is our opinionated "dev tools" widget set, which builds on the "core Bevy UI widgets" mentioned above.We're using these widgets to build the Bevy Editor, in addition to things like an ECS inspector, debug menus, etc.Bevy Rendering Devs Go Hard #This year was packed with renderer work. We landed and evolved Solari, our experimental real-time raytraced renderer (led by Jasmine):This was a MASSIVE year for GPU-driven rendering (led by @pcwalton). On modern hardware, Bevy can now handle huge scenes; drawing millions of entities at playable framerates. Our new bevy_city example is a great real world test. It procedurally generates a city with (by default) 55,000 entities (including moving cars) and it can render at 60fps! This requires no special "performance" APIs, just the standard easy-to-use data-driven Bevy APIs.We've also started landing "renderer unification" work. Bevy's 3D rendering is quite advanced at this point, and we'd like our 2D renderer to share the same infrastructure and benefit from all of the work we've done.A few days ago we fully adopted WESL shaders (migrating away from our custom-built WGSL dialect). WESL extends WGSL to support modules / imports and first class conditional compilation. It has a native Rust toolchain which builds "by default" with no specialized configuration, and we can deploy it "anywhere". We've been collaborating closely with the WESL team to shape the specification and ensure it is a great fit for Bevy.import package::{color::palette, shape::star}; import lygia::{draw::fill::fill, generative::snoise::snoise2}; import env::u; @fragment fn main(@builtin(position) pos: vec4f) -> @location(0) vec4f { let uv = pos.xy / u.resolution; var sdf = star(pos.xy, u.resolution); @if(noise) // conditions at runtime or build time sdf += snoise2(uv * 8.0 + u.time) * 0.15; let shape = fill(sdf, 0.6); return vec4f(palette(uv, u.time) * shape, shape); }The current baseline implementation is a marked improvement over the old Bevy shader experience, but this is just the beginning. They're in the process of building out features like generics, which will allow us to make high level Bevy material shaders much more accessible than they currently are. We're aiming to have a unique "best of all worlds" cohesive implementation that makes the easy stuff easy, without hiding the details away from the tinkerers (in classic Bevy fashion).We also landed a ton of renderer features: our virtual geometry ("nanite") implementation got BVH culling, we landed DLSS support, contact shadows, physically based screen space reflections, rectangular area lights, light textures, real-time filtered environment maps, vastly improved our atmosphere rendering, and fixed some of the "PBR rendering quirkiness" that has plagued us for awhile.Jackdaw: The Community-Driven Bevy Editor Experiment #This year we continued to lay the foundations for the Bevy Editor upstream. While we did this, members of the Bevy community (led by @jbuehler23) started using these foundations (BSN, Bevy Remote Protocol, Bevy UI, Bevy Feathers) to build out a functional Bevy Editor prototype called Jackdaw. Jackdaw is becoming dangerously functional:It already has a visual BSN scene editor, ECS inspection, undo/redo, a dynamic plugin / extension loading system, a material system, terrain editing, a project manager / creator, and geometry editing tooling.They've done a great job of mapping the space and exercising Bevy's foundations in practice. Once we land a couple more foundational pieces upstream (such as Assets as Entities and .bsn asset support), we'll spin up the Bevy Editor Working Group, where I plan on focusing my attention on guiding upstream Bevy Editor development, collaborating with the Jackdaw devs to take the best ideas from Jackdaw and finally for real this time build Bevy's official editor.Bevy Metrics #Tracking performance, compile time, and binary size regressions in a game engine is critical. Historically, we have done this manually "as needed". Thanks to our generous donors and François' efforts, we landed Bevy Metrics: an automated metrics system that runs on every Bevy commit, tracking Bevy's runtime performance, compile times, and binary sizes over time. This has already helped us catch a ton of regressions and will be a key piece of infrastructure for us going forward.Bevy Project Goals #Bevy development is very "ad hoc". Each individual works on what they want to, when they want to. It has historically been hard to track what is currently going on in the project, what our priorities are, what our priorities aren't, and where project leadership is currently focusing their attention. This created a lot of unnecessary tension, as contributors would often spend months building something, only to hit a wall because they built the "wrong" thing, or because project leadership didn't have the time to give the contributor's effort the attention it needed to be shepherded upstream. Additionally, Bevy community members (and people interested in Bevy) often asked for a "roadmap", and we'd say "we don't have one" and "that is not how we do things here".This year I formulated and enacted the light-weight Bevy Project Goals system, which aims to give us the tools we need to prioritize work and collaborate on that work together (check out our Contributor Guide for details). The community can propose new Goals, and we discuss those proposals on a weekly basis to decide if we want to approve, deny, or postpone them. It also allows members of project leadership (the Project Lead ... me, SMEs (Subject Matter experts), and Maintainers) the ability to "staff" Goals, which provides a signal to the community that this Goal is "fast tracked" and will receive immediate attention and stewardship.This allows leadership to be honest about its capacity (we can't "staff" everything at once) and its priorities (there are some things we must focus on, and some things we should not focus on).This is notably not a "roadmap". We aren't meaningfully planning the order of future steps ahead of time. We are just communicating the current state of things. This is also not authoritative. The Bevy community is still free to build whatever it pleases, whenever it pleases. We just now have a way to collectively decide our direction and create the necessary contribution on ramps and infrastructure to collaborate (ex: Working Groups).I am personally very happy with Goals (especially their current iteration), and believe they were an important missing piece of our workflow. The rollout wasn't quite as smooth as it should have been (which I'll touch on in the next section).Real Projects™ Using Bevy #This year we had a ton of new Bevy usage, with some exciting Steam releases, demos, and non-game apps.Toroban: an infinitely wrapping puzzle game, was released on Steam.Exofactory: a factory building game in a chill open world, made significant progress and had a ton of interesting devlogs.Jarl: a fantasy colony simulation game is running playtests at the moment.Polders, a historical Dutch city builder, continued to make significant progress this year.Wee Boats The chill multiplayer boaty honk game, now has a demo on steam!Sven is building a spaceflight simulation gameForesight (one of Bevy's biggest sponsors) is using Bevy to build Foresight Spatial Engine (already used in production) and SpatialDrive a database built for interacting with and visualizing 3D time series data.Nominal: is building hardware test apps for real-time automation, analysis, and data capture at the edge.Gob Johnson's Downhill Marmalade: a fast-paced slalom 'em up fantasy roguelite, released on Steam.Simulo, a multiplayer 2D physics sandbox, released on Steam.Insanio: an autobattler where you send misfits into vehicular combat, released on Steam.Court Wizard: A roguelite where you cast spells to defend the kingdom, was released on Steam.Willcaster: a game where you guide an ordinary frog on your magical game board, helping him with your spells, was announced on Steam.Unhaunter: the paranormal investigation simulator, made a lot of progress this year.One Planet: a political strategy game where you take on climate change, was announced on Steam.Manufact: a "design for manufacture" and simulation platform, was released. It uses Bevy as the renderer!bevy_awesome_prod has even more cool projects!There Is Always Room For Improvement #The Goal System Rollout #The initial rollout and framing of Bevy Project Goals caused some (well-founded) concern and anxiety in the community, as it was phrased in a way that made it feel "dictatorial". One of my Goals for the system was to establish "boundaries". Historically, our process (and lack thereof) organically created a culture of "build first, then yell for attention until you get it". Leadership was constantly derailing itself from its priorities to shepherd whatever happened to land on our doorstep, and this created situations such as continually promising that the Bevy Editor was a priority, yet it never manifesting over the course of many ... many years. That particular case is a complicated, multi-dimensional problem, but prioritizing the upstreaming of arbitrary unrelated work was a big piece of the problem.This culture bred toxicity in a number of ways. It created resentment in me whenever a new (very cool) thing landed on our doorstep that pulled me away from the work that I strongly believed Bevy needed. It created burnout and feelings of betrayal in contributors when their work was left unreviewed indefinitely. It created disillusionment in the wider community when critical foundational pieces (such as BSN) dragged on for years (that particular case is also multi-dimensional ... I could have pushed my work publicly years earlier and embraced public community development rather than polishing it slowly on my own).These were fundamentally problems of communication. Project leadership only has so many hours in the day. We have the right (and responsibility) to choose how we want to spend them. What the project desperately needed was a way to communicate them.Project Goals were initially framed in a way that focused on that. Preventing working from being done that wasn't "aligned" or "prioritized". Working Groups could only be created for efforts that were currently "staffed" by leadership. Goals were only "active" if they were "staffed", and "unstaffed" Goals were "inactive". While I do think this type of prioritization is necessary to a degree, it was ham-fisted and didn't properly respect Bevy's "organic development culture".We've (very recently) adopted a looser approach. "Staffed" and "unstaffed" are the states (rather than "active" and "inactive"). Working Groups can be formed for any "approved" Goal, even if it is not currently staffed. I believe this strikes the right balance. The community can propose work and collaborate on anything that is approved. We can provide these people with the centralized collaboration infrastructure they need (Working Groups), and they can make progress with or without us. However "staffing" still serves as a signal to the community as to where we are directing our focus, so it can set its expectations accordingly.AI Policy #AI has been a constant stressor on the Bevy community this year. We adopted a strict "no-AI" policy this year, which solved many problems but created many others (including fostering toxic witch hunts, incentivizing lying to maintainers, enforcement was a hard / impossible task). We are all very tired and emotionally raw.@alice-i-cecile has been working with the community (including me) to draft a new policy. I'm pretty anti-AI myself, I don't use it in my development workflows (I love my craft and don't have much interest in outsourcing it), and I am deeply concerned about the risks of AI adoption when it comes to fostering a community of competent engine developers. I think the new policy strikes the correct balance for our community. We haven't released a new policy yet (we are still working on it) and we aren't interested in starting a wider public conversation at the moment (aka: a conversation outside of the Bevy community). But I am optimistic that we are soon to be on the right track.The Bevy Foundation is (Still) Under-Funded #I outlined three paths to improve this last year: proactive fundraising, revenue generating services, and continuing to build the engine to make it more attractive and extend our reach. I didn't meaningfully do either of the first two this year. I did focus heavily on building out Bevy's foundations this year and avoiding sidetracking, and I think we are verging on a level of capability and elegance that will attract developers and funding in greater volumes. I don't think I should be focused on proactive fundraising or revenue generating services until the Bevy technology platform has reached a certain level of completeness, as that is where my competency lies, and I don't feel particularly comfortable evangelizing while there are still key pieces of the puzzle in flight.We need more full time developers so we can move faster. We need to pay our existing developers baseline salaries that encourage them to stay (rather than the ~54% paycut relative to the baseline that we are paying them today). Please help us!Did We Learn From Last Year? #It is important for organizations (and leaders) to learn from their mistakes. Here is my list of "improvement areas" from last year's birthday post, followed by how I think we handled them this year:BSN Should Have Landed FasterI believe the core issue here (@cart developing in isolation for extended periods until things are "good enough" in my eyes) has largely been addressed. BSN development over the past year has been iterative and public. My work on Assets as Entities has evolved in the open and iteratively. I've been making lots of targeted, small, but high value changes to various parts of the engine that I've been wanting to for awhile, with instant feedback loops with the community. I do daily status updates so people can track what I'm currently working on. I'll try my hardest not to slip back in to old patterns, but I'm pretty happy with how things have played out recently. I'm curious to hear what everyone else thinks about this!The Bevy Foundation is Under-FundedI discussed this above. This is still a problem! Please support our work by donating to the Bevy Foundation!Can @cart Predict The Future? #In last year's birthday post I made some predictions for the next year. Let's see how I did!BSNWe landed BSN. Score!Reactivity EcosystemBevy does have a reactivity ecosystem! There are BSN reactive impls like bevy_reactor and Jasmine's (rough / quick) reactive BSN experiment. There is also haalka, which uses "functional reactive programming" to produce its own (non-BSN, but Bevy-native) data API.We haven't yet converged on the correct upstream implementation, but I suspect this will happen within the year now that Bevy UI, Feathers, and BSN are all in a pretty solid place.Core / Standard UI WidgetsWe landed these! Another win!Baseline Editor PlatformWe did not land a baseline editor platform upstream. As mentioned above, we have made solid progress on the foundations. The ECS Inspector working group has a functional inspector implementation. Jackdaw has successfully prototyped what an editor platform could look like. We made significant, tangible, usable progress toward the goal this year. I have been saying "Bevy Editor next year" for many years now. You probably shouldn't trust me when I say it is close now. But we now have the scene system, the UI system, the editor widget library, the asset system, the remote protocol, the design language and mockups, a proven dynamic plugin loading model, and an extremely functional prototype. Additionally, we finally have a Project Lead who has run out of prerequisites to block editor progress on (well ... after Assets as Entities, but that is wrapping up now). We are well positioned to break ground. That is our (and my) next and overriding priority. We can do this!The Next Year of Bevy #The Bevy Community and I take a relatively organic and reactive approach to developing Bevy. It doesn't make sense to outline a long list of "plans" when that isn't really how development works in practice.That being said, here are some of my personal hopes, dreams, and personal priorities for the next year of Bevy:Assets as Entities: This is what I'm currently working on (with @andriyDev). It is a key piece of the editor story, as we need to be able to express complex, nested, templated assets in BSN + the Bevy Editor, and Assets as Entities is what will allow that to happen, as BSN expresses complex, nested, templated entities. It will also vastly simplify our asset system internals, make asset events "observable / react-able", and generally make assets feel more cohesive with the rest of Bevy..bsn Asset Format: BSN landed with bsn! macro support. It also landed with "runtime" support for scene assets. It didn't land with the actual .bsn asset loader. The Bevy Editor will produce .bsn files, so this is a necessary piece to land. There is a draft PR for this out, although it needs some work. We should be able to land this shortly!Upstream Bevy Editor MVP: We need this. You want this. We have proven implementations. We have prioritized progress at the cost of pretty much everything else. We are very, very close now.Reactivity Ecosystem: As mentioned above, we have explored the space, we have built the other prerequisites. I'm relatively confident we can land something this year, but I'm personally prioritizing showing upstream progress on the Bevy Editor. Reactivity is likely a part of the final UI / Editor story, but I don't think we should block on it.Excellent Shader and Material Workflows: We've been focused on modernizing the renderer and landing foundational pieces like WESL. However this has come at the cost of more user-facing shader / custom material complexity. Once the initial "2D / 3D renderer unification" work lands, I think we need to pivot our focus toward the user facing experience / lowering the accessibility bar of custom material shaders. @tychedelia has big plans for this space and I can't wait to see where this lands. WESL is a solid start, and should serve as a foundation for this work (especially as it evolves).We have plenty of other work in the pipeline, but I'm once again choosing to keep this very focused this year to convey my personal priorities.One last reminder that Bevy community members should write their own Bevy Birthday blog posts. Submit them here!If any of this excites you, we would love your help! Check out our code on GitHub and start participating in the Bevy Community.Also please consider donating to The Bevy Foundation to ensure we can continue building and leading this wildly ambitious project. The more funds we have, the more we can scale Bevy development!To many more years of Bevy!- @cartThe cute Bevy birds in this post are strongly inspired by Ed Duck's delightful Bevy bird design

blocks.html_en: BSN #
This year we finally landed BSN: Bevy's next generation scene system:

sentences.en: This year we finally landed BSN: Bevy's next generation scene system:
sentences.zh: 今年我们终于落地了BSN：Bevy的下一代场景系统：

blocks.html_en: This was a massive step forward for Bevy's usability. It enables developers to quickly and easily spawn composable, inheritable, interrelated hierarchies of ECS entities and components in a templated, dependency and asset-aware way (some engines call these "prefabs" instead of "scenes"). Developers can compose BSN within their Rust code using the bsn! macro, or they can define it in asset files (the .bsn asset format should land on Bevy main soon).

sentences.en: This was a massive step forward for Bevy's usability.
sentences.zh: 这对于 Bevy 的可用性来说是一个巨大的进步。

sentences.en: It enables developers to quickly and easily spawn composable, inheritable, interrelated hierarchies of ECS entities and components in a templated, dependency and asset-aware way (some engines call these "prefabs" instead of "scenes").
sentences.zh: 它使开发人员能够以模板化、依赖关系和资产感知的方式快速轻松地生成 ECS 实体和组件的可组合、可继承、相互关联的层次结构（某些引擎将这些称为“预制件”而不是“场景”）。

sentences.en: Developers can compose BSN within their Rust code using the bsn!
sentences.zh: 开发人员可以使用 bsn! 在他们的 Rust 代码中编写 BSN！

sentences.en: macro, or they can define it in asset files (the .bsn asset format should land on Bevy main soon).
sentences.zh: 宏，或者他们可以在资产文件中定义它（.bsn 资产格式应该很快就会登陆 Bevy main）。

blocks.html_en: BSN is also a key piece of Bevy's UI story going forward. UI developers (especially outside of the engine space) expect a certain level of ergonomics that raw Rust cannot provide. With BSN, composing UI in Bevy has never been easier!

blocks.html_en: Bevy development is very "ad hoc". Each individual works on what they want to, when they want to. It has historically been hard to track what is currently going on in the project, what our priorities are, what our priorities aren't, and where project leadership is currently focusing their attention. This created a lot of unnecessary tension, as contributors would often spend months building something, only to hit a wall because they built the "wrong" thing, or because project leadership didn't have the time to give the contributor's effort the attention it needed to be shepherded upstream. Additionally, Bevy community members (and people interested in Bevy) often asked for a "roadmap", and we'd say "we don't have one" and "that is not how we do things here".

blocks.html_en: This year I formulated and enacted the light-weight Bevy Project Goals system, which aims to give us the tools we need to prioritize work and collaborate on that work together (check out our Contributor Guide for details). The community can propose new Goals, and we discuss those proposals on a weekly basis to decide if we want to approve, deny, or postpone them. It also allows members of project leadership (the Project Lead ... me, SMEs (Subject Matter experts), and Maintainers) the ability to "staff" Goals, which provides a signal to the community that this Goal is "fast tracked" and will receive immediate attention and stewardship.

blocks.html_en: The initial rollout and framing of Bevy Project Goals caused some (well-founded) concern and anxiety in the community, as it was phrased in a way that made it feel "dictatorial". One of my Goals for the system was to establish "boundaries". Historically, our process (and lack thereof) organically created a culture of "build first, then yell for attention until you get it". Leadership was constantly derailing itself from its priorities to shepherd whatever happened to land on our doorstep, and this created situations such as continually promising that the Bevy Editor was a priority, yet it never manifesting over the course of many ... many years. That particular case is a complicated, multi-dimensional problem, but prioritizing the upstreaming of arbitrary unrelated work was a big piece of the problem.

It created disillusionment in the wider community when critical foundational pieces (such as BSN) dragged on for years (that particular case is also multi-dimensional ... I could have pushed my work publicly years earlier and embraced public community development rather than polishing it slowly on my own).

blocks.html_en: AI has been a constant stressor on the Bevy community this year. We adopted a strict "no-AI" policy this year, which solved many problems but created many others (including fostering toxic witch hunts, incentivizing lying to maintainers, enforcement was a hard / impossible task). We are all very tired and emotionally raw.

sentences.en: AI has been a constant stressor on the Bevy community this year.

blocks.html_en: @alice-i-cecile has been working with the community (including me) to draft a new policy. I'm pretty anti-AI myself, I don't use it in my development workflows (I love my craft and don't have much interest in outsourcing it), and I am deeply concerned about the risks of AI adoption when it comes to fostering a community of competent engine developers. I think the new policy strikes the correct balance for our community. We haven't released a new policy yet (we are still working on it) and we aren't interested in starting a wider public conversation at the moment (aka: a conversation outside of the Bevy community). But I am optimistic that we are soon to be on the right track.

blocks.html_en: I outlined three paths to improve this last year: proactive fundraising, revenue generating services, and continuing to build the engine to make it more attractive and extend our reach. I didn't meaningfully do either of the first two this year. I did focus heavily on building out Bevy's foundations this year and avoiding sidetracking, and I think we are verging on a level of capability and elegance that will attract developers and funding in greater volumes. blocks.html_en: We did not land a baseline editor platform upstream. As mentioned above, we have made solid progress on the foundations. The ECS Inspector working group has a functional inspector implementation. Jackdaw has successfully prototyped what an editor platform could look like. We made significant, tangible, usable progress toward the goal this year. I have been saying "Bevy Editor next year" for many years now. You probably shouldn't trust me when I say it is close now. But we now have the scene system, the UI system, the editor widget library, the asset system, the remote protocol, the design language and mockups, a proven dynamic plugin loading model, and an extremely functional prototype. Additionally, we finally have a Project Lead who has run out of prerequisites to block editor progress on (well ... after Assets as Entities, but that is wrapping up now). 嘿！ @cart 这里（Bevy 的创建者和项目负责人）。 说起来很疯狂，但贝维现在已经六岁了！

按照惯例，我将借此机会回顾过去的一年，勾画我们对未来的希望和梦想。 如果您好奇，请查看 Bevy 的一岁、二岁、三岁、四岁和五岁生日帖子。

我强烈鼓励 Bevy 开发者和社区成员撰写自己的 Bevy 六岁生日反思帖子。 只需在某处发布您的帖子（如果您愿意，也可以发布到社交媒体）并在此处链接到它。 一个月后，我们将发布一篇“反思贝维的第六年”汇总帖子，将这些内容汇总到一个地方。 这是我们作为一个社区庆祝我们的胜利、确定改进领域并校准我们明年的道路的机会。

对于那些不知道的人来说，Bevy 是一个令人耳目一新的简单数据驱动游戏引擎和使用 Rust 构建的应用程序框架。 Bevy 也是永久免费且开源的！ 您可以在 GitHub 上获取完整的源代码。 我们有一个快速入门指南。 您可以查看 Bevy Assets，获取社区开发的插件、板条箱、游戏和学习资源库。

这一切都归功于贝维基金会的慷慨捐助者。 如果您喜欢 Bevy，请考虑支持我们的工作！ 每一笔捐款都直接用于改善每个人的 Bevy，而我们的资金严重不足，无法实现我们的雄心壮志。

具有里程碑意义的一年#

  • 8 月 25 日：Bevy Merch 我们推出了新的 Bevy Merch 商店，以便 Bevy 开发者可以表达他们的支持。 请注意，我们每笔销售仅赚取 3 美元... 这家商店的主要目的是让人们在野外代表 Bevy，而不是成为资金来源。
  • 9 月 30 日：Bevy 0.17 我们推出了 Solari / 光线追踪照明、改进的观察者/事件、核心 Bevy UI 小部件、Bevy Feathers、Rust Hotpatching、光照纹理、DLSS、Tilemap 块渲染、Web 托管资源加载、反射自动注册、帧时间图、UI 渐变、Raymarched 氛围、虚拟几何、BVH 剔除等等！
  • 12 月 10 日：Bevy 指标 感谢我们慷慨的捐助者和 François 的努力，我们实现了一个自动化指标系统，该系统在每次 Bevy 提交上运行，随着时间的推移跟踪 Bevy 的运行时性能、编译时间和二进制大小。 这帮助我们发现了大量的回归问题，并将成为我们未来发展的关键基础设施。
  • 1 月 13 日：Bevy 0.18 我们推出了大气遮挡和 PBR 着色、广义大气散射媒体、Solari 改进、PBR 着色修复、字体变化、自动定向导航、全屏材质、货物特征集合、第一方相机控制器等等！

  • 6 月：Bevy 在 crates.io 上的下载量达到 6,000,000 次！
  • 6 月 19 日：Bevy 0.19 我们推出了下一代场景/BSN、更快地渲染更大的场景、接触阴影、更多羽毛小部件、文本输入、更丰富的文本、应用程序设置、后处理效果、改进的蒙皮网格剔除等等！

我感到自豪的事情#

我总是尽量不在这里重复自己，但请注意，我仍然对我在贝维的第一个、第二个、第三个、第四个和第五个生日帖子中概述的事情感到非常自豪。

BSN #

今年我们终于落地了BSN：Bevy的下一代场景系统：

这对于 Bevy 的可用性来说是一个巨大的进步。 它使开发人员能够以模板化、依赖关系和资产感知的方式快速轻松地生成 ECS 实体和组件的可组合、可继承、相互关联的层次结构（某些引擎将这些称为“预制件”而不是“场景”）。 开发人员可以使用 bsn! 在他们的 Rust 代码中编写 BSN！ 宏，或者他们可以在资产文件中定义它（.bsn 资产格式应该很快就会登陆 Bevy main）。

BSN 也是 Bevy 未来 UI 故事的关键部分。 UI 开发人员（尤其是引擎领域之外的开发人员）期望达到原始 Rust 无法提供的一定程度的人体工程学效果。 借助 BSN，在 Bevy 中编写 UI 从未如此简单！

fn button() -> impl Scene {
    bsn! {
        Node { width: px(200), height: px(100) }
        on(|press: On<PointerPress>| info!("pressed!"))
        Children [
            Text("Button")
        ]
    }
}

与其他流行的 UI 框架不同，BSN 是一个由 ECS 驱动的通用数据层，对于游戏逻辑、通用应用程序逻辑和 UI 逻辑同样有用。

BSN 对于即将推出的 Bevy 编辑器至关重要，它将是一个构建在 Bevy UI + BSN 之上的普通 Bevy 应用程序。 Bevy 编辑器还将通过视觉场景编辑器组成 BSN 资产。

我真的很高兴看到人们在野外享受 BSN。 Exofactory 的开发人员将其生成代码移植到 BSN 后节省了 7,364 行代码。 BSN 对我来说是一个多年的项目，最终从中获得“现实世界”的价值感觉真好。

我将在博客文章中解释 BSN 详细信息，但对于 Bevy 开发者来说，这是一个激动人心的时刻！

贝维用户界面#

Bevy 的 UI 故事今年取得了长足的进步。 除了登陆 BSN 之外，我们还登陆了“核心 Bevy UI 小部件”，它们是仅行为的“无样式”小部件，旨在用作样式/更高级别小部件的共享基线。 将 Button 小部件添加到您的实体中，它开始表现得像一个按钮，具有按钮事件、按下和悬停状态、键盘快捷键和辅助功能！

fn button() -> impl Scene {
    bsn! { 
        Button
        Node { width: px(200), height: px(100) }
        on(|activate: On<Activate>| {
            info!("Button activated!")
        })
    }
}

我们登陆了按钮、复选框、单选按钮、列表、滚动区域/滚动条、滑块、模式对话框、菜单和弹出窗口。 我们最终还推出了一个上游文本输入小部件：

Bevy UI 现在还支持渐变、每侧 UI 边框颜色、文本背景颜色、自动定向导航、删除线、下划线、粗细和连字等字体变化、可变字体属性以及更好的字体选择。

Bevy UI 领域的一切开始变得非常实用！

群羽毛#

我们还在今年年初推出了 Bevy Feathers（由 Talin 领导），然后全年对其进行了重大改进和扩展。 Bevy Feathers 是我们固执己见的“开发工具”小部件集，它建立在上面提到的“核心 Bevy UI 小部件”之上。

除了 ECS 检查器、调试菜单等之外，我们还使用这些小部件来构建 Bevy 编辑器。

Bevy 渲染开发人员努力#

今年充满了渲染器工作。 我们登陆并改进了 Solari，我们的实验性实时光线追踪渲染器（由 Jasmine 领导）：

对于 GPU 驱动的渲染来说，今年是意义重大的一年（由 @pcwalton 领导）。 在现代硬件上，Bevy 现在可以处理巨大的场景；以可播放的帧速率绘制数百万个实体。 我们的新 bevy_city 示例是一个很棒的现实世界测试。 它按程序生成一个城市（默认情况下）有 55,000 个实体（包括移动的汽车），并且可以以 60 fps 渲染！ 这不需要特殊的“性能”API，只需要标准的易于使用的数据驱动的 Bevy API。

我们还开始开展“渲染器统一”工作。 Bevy 的 3D 渲染在这一点上相当先进，我们希望我们的 2D 渲染器能够共享相同的基础设施，并从我们所做的所有工作中受益。

几天前，我们完全采用了 WESL 着色器（远离我们定制的 WGSL 方言）。 WESL 扩展了 WGSL 以支持模块/导入和一流的条件编译。 它有一个原生 Rust 工具链，“默认”构建，无需专门配置，我们可以将其部署在“任何地方”。 我们一直与 WESL 团队密切合作来制定规范并确保它非常适合 Bevy。

import package::{color::palette, shape::star};
import lygia::{draw::fill::fill, generative::snoise::snoise2};
import env::u;

@fragment
fn main(@builtin(position) pos: vec4f) -> @location(0) vec4f {
  let uv = pos.xy / u.resolution;
  var sdf = star(pos.xy, u.resolution);

  @if(noise)  // conditions at runtime or build time
  sdf += snoise2(uv * 8.0 + u.time) * 0.15;

  let shape = fill(sdf, 0.6);
  return vec4f(palette(uv, u.time) * shape, shape);
}

当前的基线实现比旧的 Bevy 着色器体验有了显着改进，但这仅仅是开始。 他们正在构建诸如泛型之类的功能，这将使我们能够使高级 Bevy 材质着色器比目前更容易使用。 我们的目标是拥有一个独特的“世界上最好的”凝聚力实现，使简单的事情变得简单，而不向修补者隐藏细​​节（​​以经典的 Bevy 方式）。

我们还实现了大量的渲染器功能：我们的虚拟几何（“nanite”）实现得到了 BVH 剔除，我们实现了 DLSS 支持、接触阴影、基于物理的屏幕空间反射、矩形区域光、光照纹理、实时过滤的环境贴图，极大地改进了我们的气氛渲染，并修复了一些困扰我们一段时间的“PBR 渲染怪癖”。

Jackdaw：社区驱动的 Bevy 编辑器实验 #

今年我们继续为 Bevy Editor 上游奠定基础。 当我们这样做时，Bevy 社区的成员（由 @jbuehler23 领导）开始使用这些基础（BSN、Bevy 远程协议、Bevy UI、Bevy Feathers）来构建一个名为 Jackdaw 的功能性 Bevy 编辑器原型。 寒鸦的功能正在变得危险：

它已经拥有可视化 BSN 场景编辑器、ECS 检查、撤消/重做、动态插件/扩展加载系统、材质系统、地形编辑、项目管理器/创建器和几何编辑工具。

他们在绘制空间图和在实践中运用贝维的基础方面做得非常出色。 一旦我们在上游找到了更多基础部分（例如作为实体的资产和 .bsn 资产支持），我们将启动 Bevy 编辑器工作组，我计划将注意力集中在指导上游 Bevy 编辑器开发上，与 Jackdaw 开发人员合作，从 Jackdaw 中汲取最佳想法，最后这次真正构建 Bevy 的官方编辑器。

贝维指标#

跟踪游戏引擎中的性能、编译时间和二进制大小回归至关重要。 从历史上看，我们“根据需要”手动完成此操作。 感谢我们慷慨的捐助者和 François 的努力，我们推出了 Bevy Metrics：一个在每次 Bevy 提交上运行的自动化指标系统，随着时间的推移跟踪 Bevy 的运行时性能、编译时间和二进制大小。 这已经帮助我们发现了大量的回归问题，并将成为我们未来发展的关键基础设施。

Bevy 项目目标#

Bevy 的开发是非常“临时”的。 每个人都可以在自己愿意的时候做自己想做的事。 从历史上看，很难跟踪项目中当前正在发生的事情、我们的优先事项是什么、我们的优先事项不是什么，以及项目领导目前的注意力集中在哪里。 这造成了很多不必要的紧张，因为贡献者经常花费几个月的时间来构建一些东西，却因为构建了“错误”的东西而碰壁，或者因为项目领导没有时间给予贡献者的努力以引导上游所需的注意力。 此外，Bevy 社区成员（以及对 Bevy 感兴趣的人）经常要求提供“路线图”，而我们会说“我们没有”和“这不是我们在这里做事的方式”。

今年，我制定并颁布了轻量级的 Bevy 项目目标系统，该系统旨在为我们提供确定工作优先级并共同协作所需的工具（有关详细信息，请查看我们的贡献者指南）。 社区可以提出新的目标，我们每周讨论这些提案，以决定是否要批准、拒绝或推迟它们。 它还允许项目领导成员（Project Lead ... 我、中小企业（主题专家）和维护者）“配备”目标的能力，这向社区发出一个信号，表明该目标正在“快速跟踪”并将立即受到关注和管理。

这使得领导层能够诚实地对待自己的能力（我们不能同时为所有事情配备“人员”）和优先事项（有些事情我们必须关注，有些事情我们不应该关注）。

值得注意的是，这不是一个“路线图”。 我们并没有提前有意义地计划未来步骤的顺序。 我们只是传达当前的情况。 这也并不具有权威性。 Bevy 社区仍然可以随时随地自由地构建任何它喜欢的东西。 我们现在有了一种方法来集体决定我们的方向，并在坡道和基础设施方面做出必要的贡献以进行合作（例如：工作组）。

我个人对目标（尤其是当前的迭代）非常满意，并相信它们是我们工作流程中重要的缺失部分。 推出并不像应有的那么顺利（我将在下一节中谈到）。

总是有改进的空间#

目标系统推出#

Bevy 项目目标的最初推出和框架在社区中引起了一些（有充分根据的）担忧和焦虑，因为它的措辞方式让人感觉“独裁”。 我对该系统的目标之一是建立“边界”。 从历史上看，我们的流程（以及缺乏流程）有机地创造了一种“先构建，然后大喊大叫以引起关注，直到你得到它”的文化。 领导层不断地偏离其优先事项，以引导发生在我们家门口的任何事情，这造成了诸如不断承诺 Bevy 编辑是优先事项之类的情况，但它从未在许多过程中体现出来...... 很多年了。 这种特殊情况是一个复杂的多维问题，但优先考虑任意不相关工作的上游是一个大问题。

这种文化通过多种方式产生了毒性。 每当一件新的（非常酷的）东西落在我们家门口，让我远离我坚信贝维需要的工作时，我就会产生怨恨。 当贡献者的工作得不到无限期的审查时，就会产生倦怠感和被背叛的感觉。 当关键的基础部分（例如 BSN）拖延多年（这种特殊情况也是多维的……）时，它在更广泛的社区中造成了幻灭。 我本可以早几年公开推动我的工作并接受公共社区的发展，而不是自己慢慢完善它）。

这些从根本上来说是沟通问题。 项目领导一天只有这么多时间。 我们有权利（和责任）选择如何使用它们。 该项目迫切需要一种沟通方式。

项目目标最初是以此为重点制定的。 防止完成未“一致”或“优先”的工作。 只能为目前由领导层“配备”的工作创建工作组。 只有“有人值守”的目标才“活跃”，而“无人值守”的目标则“不活跃”。 虽然我确实认为这种优先顺序在某种程度上是必要的，但它是笨拙的，并且没有适当尊重贝维的“有机发展文化”。

我们（最近）采取了更为宽松的方法。 “有人值守”和“无人值守”是状态（而不是“活动”和“不活动”）。 可以为任何“批准的”目标组建工作组，即使目前没有人员配备。 我相信这达到了正确的平衡。 社区可以提出工作建议并就任何获得批准的事项进行协作。 我们可以为这些人提供他们所需的集中协作基础设施（工作组），无论有没有我们，他们都可以取得进展。 然而，“人员配备”仍然是向社区发出的信号，表明我们的重点方向，因此社区可以相应地设定其期望。

人工智能政策#

今年，人工智能一直是 Bevy 社区的一个持续压力源。 我们今年采取了严格的“无人工智能”政策，解决了许多问题，但也造成了许多其他问题（包括助长有毒的政治迫害、激励对维护者撒谎、执行是一项艰巨/不可能的任务）。 我们都很累，情绪也很脆弱。

@alice-i-cecile 一直在与社区（包括我）合作起草一项新政策。 我自己非常反对人工智能，我不会在我的开发工作流程中使用它（我喜欢我的手艺，并且对外包它没有太大兴趣），并且在培养有能力的引擎开发人员社区时，我非常担心采用人工智能的风险。 我认为新政策为我们的社区实现了正确的平衡。 我们还没有发布新政策（我们仍在研究中），并且我们目前没有兴趣开始更广泛的公共对话（又名：Bevy 社区之外的对话）。 但我乐观地认为我们很快就会走上正轨。

Bevy 基金会（仍然）资金不足#

去年，我概述了改善这一状况的三种途径：积极筹款、创收服务以及继续打造引擎以使其更具吸引力并扩大我们的影响力。 今年前两项我都没有有意义地去做。 今年我确实重点关注了 Bevy 的基础建设并避免偏离轨道，我认为我们的能力和优雅水平已接近尾声，这将吸引更多的开发人员和资金。 在 Bevy 技术平台达到一定程度的完整性之前，我认为我不应该专注于主动筹款或创收服务，因为这就是我的能力所在，而且当难题的关键部分仍然存在时，我对传播福音感到不太舒服。

我们需要更多全职开发人员，以便我们能够更快地行动。 我们需要向现有开发人员支付基准工资，以鼓励他们留下来（而不是相对于我们今天支付给他们的基准工资削减约 54%）。 请帮助我们！

基线编辑平台

我们没有在上游建立基线编辑器平台。 如上所述，我们在基础上取得了扎实的进展。 ECS Inspector 工作组有一个功能性检查器实现。 Jackdaw 已成功构建了编辑器平台的原型。 今年我们在实现这一目标方面取得了重大、切实、可用的进展。 多年来我一直在说“明年请编辑”。 当我说现在已经很接近时，你可能不应该相信我。 但我们现在拥有场景系统、UI 系统、编辑器小部件库、资产系统、远程协议、设计语言和模型、经过验证的动态插件加载模型以及功能极其强大的原型。 此外，我们终于有了一位项目负责人，他已经满足了阻止编辑器进度的先决条件（嗯...... 在资产作为实体之后，但现在已经结束了）。 我们已做好破土动工的准备。 这是我们（和我的）下一个首要任务。 我们可以做到这一点！

贝维的明年#

Bevy 社区和我采用相对有机和反应性的方法来开发 Bevy。 当开发实际上并非如此时，列出一长串“计划”是没有意义的。

话虽这么说，以下是我对贝维明年的一些个人希望、梦想和个人优先事项：

  • 资产作为实体：这就是我目前正在研究的内容（与@andriyDev）。 这是编辑器故事的关键部分，因为我们需要能够在 BSN + Bevy 编辑器中表达复杂的、嵌套的、模板化的资产，而资产作为实体将允许这种情况发生，因为 BSN 表达复杂的、嵌套的、模板化的实体。 它还将极大地简化我们的资产系统内部结构，使资产事件“可观察/可反应”，并且通常使资产与 Bevy 的其他部分更具凝聚力。
  • .bsn 资产格式：BSN 登陆 bsn！ 宏观支持。 它还提供了对场景资产的“运行时”支持。 它没有与实际的 .bsn 资源加载器一起登陆。 Bevy 编辑器将生成 .bsn 文件，因此这是落地的必要部分。 尽管还需要一些工作，但已经有一份 PR 草案。 我们应该很快就能着陆！
  • 上游 Bevy 编辑 MVP：我们需要这个。 你想要这个。 我们有经过验证的实施。 我们以牺牲几乎所有其他事情为代价来优先考虑进展。 我们现在非常非常接近。
  • 反应性生态系统：如上所述，我们已经探索了这个空间，我们已经建立了其他先决条件。 我相对有信心我们今年能取得一些成果，但我个人优先考虑在 Bevy 编辑器上展示上游进展。 反应性可能是最终 UI/编辑器故事的一部分，但我认为我们不应该阻止它。
  • 出色的着色器和材质工作流程：我们一直专注于渲染器的现代化和落地基础部分，例如 WESL。 然而，这是以更多面向用户的着色器/自定义材质复杂性为代价的。 一旦最初的“2D / 3D 渲染器统一”工作落地，我认为我们需要将重点转向面向用户的体验/降低自定义材质着色器的可访问性。 @tychedelia 对这个空间有宏伟的计划，我迫不及待地想看看它会落到哪里。 WESL 是一个坚实的开始，并且应该作为这项工作的基础（尤其是随着它的发展）。

我们还有很多其他工作正在进行中，但今年我再次选择集中精力来传达我个人的优先事项。
